column2: Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the highest of men,
and to the goddess Sarasvatī as well, one should then recite the Jaya.
Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a bard versed in the ancient lore, at the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, the master of the house, in the Naimiṣa Forest,
came up to the brahmin seers of strict vows as they sat at their ease,
bowed low in humility, one day, the son of the bard.
When he had reached the hermitage, the dwellers of the Naimiṣa Forest,
the ascetics, gathered round him there to hear his wondrous tales.
Greeting all those hermits with joined palms,
he asked after the growth of their austerities, and the good ones welcomed him.
Then, when all those ascetics had sat down,
Lomaharṣaṇa's son humbly took the seat that was shown him.
Seeing him seated at his ease and rested,
a certain seer there asked him, to set the tales going:

From where do you come, Sauti, and where have you spent
7.2	this time, lotus-eyed one? Tell me, who ask you this.

At the snake sacrifice of the great-souled royal seer Janamejaya,
8.2	in the presence of that lord of kings, the true son of Parikṣit,
9.1	the many holy tales proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
9.2	which Vaiśaṃpāyana duly told there —
10.1	when I had heard them, tales of wondrous meaning that belong to the Mahābhārata,
10.2	and had wandered round many fords and sanctuaries,
11.1	to the holy place called Samantapañcaka, frequented by the twice-born,
11.2	I went, to the land where long ago the war was fought
11.3	between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus and all the kings.
12.1	Wishing to see you, I have come from there into your presence here.
12.2	Long-lived ones, all of you I hold to be one with Brahman.
13.1	At this sacrifice, most fortunate ones, radiant as the sun and fire,
13.2	bathed and pure, your prayers muttered, your fires fed,
13.3	you sit at your ease. What shall I tell you, twice-born?
14.1	Holy tales founded on the ancient lore, or tales founded on dharma,
14.2	or the deeds of the lords of men and of the great-souled seers?

The ancient lore proclaimed by Dvaipāyana, the supreme seer,
15.2	which the gods and the brahmin seers honoured when they heard it,
16.1	of that best of narratives, wondrous in its words and books,
16.2	endowed with subtle meanings and reasoning, adorned with the meanings of the Veda,
17.1	of the history of the Bhāratas — the holy collection, rich in the book's meanings,
17.2	refined, sacred, amplified by many treatises,
18.1	which Vaiśaṃpāyana told King Janamejaya,
18.2	duly, that seer, gladly, at the session, at Dvaipāyana's command,
19.1	the equal of the four Vedas, the work of Vyāsa of wondrous deeds —
19.2	that collection we wish to hear, righteous, dispelling the fear of evil.

The first Person, the Lord, much invoked, much praised,
20.2	the Truth, the one imperishable syllable, Brahman, manifest and unmanifest, eternal,
21.1	non-being and being, and the universe; beyond being and non-being,
21.2	creator of the high and the low, ancient, supreme, imperishable,
22.1	auspicious, the auspicious one, Viṣṇu, most desired, sinless, pure,
22.2	Hṛṣīkeśa, Hari, guru of all that moves and does not move — having bowed to him,
23.1	the thought of the great seer honoured here in all the world, the great-souled,
23.2	of Vyāsa of boundless splendour, I shall proclaim entire.
24.1	Some poets have told this history, others tell it now,
24.2	and others again will tell it on earth.
25.1	This great knowledge is established in the three worlds,
25.2	and the twice-born keep it, in full and in brief;
26.1	adorned with fine words, with the usages of gods and men,
26.2	set in metres of many kinds, it is dear to the learned.
27.1	When this world was without radiance, without light, covered on every side by darkness,
27.2	there came to be one great egg, the imperishable seed of creatures,
28.1	at the beginning of the age, the great divine cause, as they say,
28.2	in which, it is heard, is the True, the Light, the eternal Brahman,
29.1	wondrous and inconceivable, the same in every part,
29.2	the unmanifest, subtle cause, whose nature is being and non-being.
30.1	From it was born the Grandfather, the sole lord Prajāpati,
30.2	Brahmā, guru of the gods, Sthāṇu, Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin,
31.1	Dakṣa the son of Pracetas, and the seven sons of Dakṣa;
31.2	then came forth the lords of creatures, twenty-one of them,
32.1	and the Person of immeasurable soul, whom all the seers know,
32.2	the All-Gods, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins,
33.1	Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and the Fathers;
33.2	then were born the learned, cultivated, stainless brahmin seers,
34.1	and many royal seers, endowed with every virtue;
34.2	the waters, the sky, the earth, the wind, the middle air, and the directions,
35.1	the year, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, days and nights in their order,
35.2	and whatever else there is — all of it came to be, with the world as its witness.
36.1	Whatever is seen here, any creature, moving or unmoving,
36.2	is all drawn in again when the end of the age arrives.
37.1	As in its turn each season shows its signs, of many forms,
37.2	the very same ones, so do beings appear at the beginnings of the ages.
38.1	Thus this wheel, without beginning or end, that brings about the dissolution of creatures,
38.2	never born and never dying, turns round and round in the world.
39.1	Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
39.2	and thirty-three: the creation of the gods, told in brief.
40.1	The son of Heaven, Bṛhadbhānu, Cakṣus, Ātman, Vibhāvasu,
40.2	Savitṛ, Ṛcīka, Arka, Bhānu, Āśāvaha, Ravi —
